Sirius.summary: The brightest star in our night sky is about 8.6 light-years away and has a faint stellar companion, Sirius B.
Sirius.findTip: Look for the standout bright star in Canis Major.

Polaris.summary: The North Star lies close to the north celestial pole, so it moves very little through the night.
Polaris.findTip: Follow the two outer stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl toward the end of the Little Dipper’s handle.

Vega.summary: A hydrogen-fusing star about 25 light-years away; one corner of the Summer Triangle.
Vega.findTip: Start with the bright star in Lyra, then compare its triangle with Deneb and Altair.

Altair.summary: A nearby hydrogen-fusing star, about 17 light-years away, in Aquila.
Altair.findTip: It marks one corner of the Summer Triangle with Vega and Deneb.

Deneb.summary: A luminous supergiant marking the tail of Cygnus, the Swan.
Deneb.findTip: Follow the long axis of the Northern Cross from Deneb toward Albireo.

Betelgeuse.summary: A red supergiant marking one shoulder of Orion.
Betelgeuse.findTip: Compare its reddish color with blue-white Rigel across Orion’s belt.

Rigel.summary: A blue supergiant marking one of Orion’s feet.
Rigel.findTip: Look across Orion’s three-star belt from reddish Betelgeuse.

Capella.summary: Auriga’s brightest star. It does not have a nearby partner as conspicuous as Gemini’s Castor–Pollux pair.
Capella.findTip: Use Orion and the Castor–Pollux pair to avoid confusing Auriga with Gemini.

Pollux.summary: The brighter of Gemini’s two head stars, about 34 light-years away. It has a known giant planet.
Pollux.findTip: Find the bright paired stars Castor and Pollux at the heads of Gemini.

Castor.summary: Gemini’s slightly fainter head star is actually a six-star system, about 51 light-years away.
Castor.findTip: Find its bright partner Pollux; together they mark the Twins’ heads.

Aldebaran.summary: This orange star appears among the V-shaped Hyades but is a foreground star, not a cluster member.
Aldebaran.findTip: Look for the conspicuous orange point in Taurus’s V-shaped face.

Procyon.summary: One of the three bright landmarks of the Winter Triangle.
Procyon.findTip: Connect it with Sirius and Betelgeuse to trace the triangle.

Arcturus.summary: A bright landmark star in Boötes.
Arcturus.findTip: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper’s handle outward toward Arcturus.

Spica.summary: Virgo’s bright anchor star and a corner of the Diamond of Virgo.
Spica.findTip: Compare its position with Arcturus, Denebola and Cor Caroli to trace the diamond.

Regulus.summary: Leo’s bright landmark sits at the base of its recognizable Sickle pattern.
Regulus.findTip: Find the curved Sickle, shaped like a backward question mark.

Antares.summary: A red supergiant in the heart of Scorpius. Its atmosphere is vastly larger than the Sun’s.
Antares.findTip: Look for the red-tinted bright star within the Scorpion’s pattern.

Fomalhaut.summary: A nearby star system about 25 light-years away. Hubble has studied dust around it.
Fomalhaut.findTip: Use the chart’s bearing to locate it in the southern part of the sky.

Alpheratz.summary: One of the four corners of the Great Square of Pegasus.
Alpheratz.findTip: Find the large square formed with Scheat, Markab and Algenib.

Mirach.summary: The middle of Andromeda’s prominent chain of Alpheratz, Mirach and Almach.
Mirach.findTip: Trace Andromeda’s chain outward from the Great Square of Pegasus.

Almach.summary: A bright anchor at the far end of Andromeda’s prominent three-star chain.
Almach.findTip: Follow Alpheratz through Mirach to Almach.

Orion.summary: The Hunter contains red Betelgeuse, blue Rigel and a distinctive three-star belt.
Orion.findTip: Start with the belt; its bright surrounding stars outline the body.

Ursa Major.summary: The Great Bear contains the familiar Big Dipper pattern.
Ursa Major.findTip: The two stars at the outer end of the Dipper’s bowl point toward Polaris.

Ursa Minor.summary: The Little Bear contains the Little Dipper and the North Star.
Ursa Minor.findTip: Polaris marks the tip of the Little Dipper’s handle.

Cassiopeia.summary: Five conspicuous stars make its recognizable W-shaped pattern.
Cassiopeia.findTip: Search for the W in the northern sky; its tilt changes as the sky turns.

Cygnus.summary: The Swan’s brightest stars make the Northern Cross.
Cygnus.findTip: Start at Deneb, its tail, and follow the body toward Albireo; the crossbar forms the wings.

Lyra.summary: The Harp is a small constellation anchored by brilliant Vega.
Lyra.findTip: Find Vega first; it is a corner of the much larger Summer Triangle.

Aquila.summary: The Eagle is anchored by Altair, a Summer Triangle star.
Aquila.findTip: Locate Altair using Vega and Deneb as the other two triangle corners.

Taurus.summary: The Bull’s face includes the V-shaped Hyades, with orange Aldebaran appearing in front of that cluster.
Taurus.findTip: Find Aldebaran, trace the V, then look nearby for the compact Pleiades cluster.

Gemini.summary: The Twins have two conspicuous head stars: Castor and Pollux.
Gemini.findTip: Continue from Rigel through Orion’s belt and Betelgeuse toward the pair.

Scorpius.summary: The Scorpion has red Antares at its heart.
Scorpius.findTip: Begin with Antares and trace the connected stars of the Scorpion.

Leo.summary: The Lion’s Sickle is one of its easiest patterns to recognize.
Leo.findTip: Find bright Regulus at the bottom of the backward-question-mark shape.

Pegasus.summary: Its Great Square is a large landmark made by Scheat, Alpheratz, Markab and Algenib.
Pegasus.findTip: Find the four widely spaced corners before tracing the remaining figure.

Andromeda.summary: This constellation contains the Andromeda Galaxy, our nearest large galactic neighbor.
Andromeda.findTip: Use the Great Square or Cassiopeia to find the area. The galaxy needs a darker sky than the main stars.

Mercury.summary: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun.
Mercury.findTip: Usually a twilight target close to the horizon. Never sweep near the Sun with binoculars or a telescope.

Venus.summary: An Earth-sized rocky world with a dense atmosphere; it is the hottest planet.
Venus.findTip: Look for a very bright point in the morning or evening sky. Never aim optics toward the Sun.

Mars.summary: Iron minerals rusting in its rocks and dust give Mars its reddish appearance.
Mars.findTip: Look for a warm-colored point and match its exact charted position.

Jupiter.summary: A gas giant with four large Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Jupiter.findTip: Binoculars or a small telescope can reveal its large moons when conditions allow.

Saturn.summary: A giant planet surrounded by a broad system of rings.
Saturn.findTip: A small telescope can reveal the rings; the unaided eye sees a point of light.

Uranus.summary: A faint outer planet at the edge of unaided-eye visibility under very dark skies.
Uranus.findTip: Use binoculars or a telescope and compare carefully with nearby charted stars.

Neptune.summary: Too faint to see with the unaided eye.
Neptune.findTip: Use a telescope or high-powered binoculars and a detailed star chart; a plotted position is not a naked-eye sighting.

Moon.summary: The Moon turns once per orbit, keeping roughly the same side facing Earth. Its changing sunlit portion produces the phases.
Moon.findTip: The border between light and dark brings out crater shadows particularly well.

Sun.summary: Our solar system’s star is a hot ball of hydrogen and helium whose energy powers life on Earth.
Sun.findTip: Never look directly at the Sun or point unfiltered binoculars or a telescope at it.
